title: no_std: a tiny kernel and bare metal
summary: What std is made of (core, alloc and the OS layer), freestanding programs with no_std and no_main, the panic handler and the _start entry point, Rust in Action's FledgeOS writing to the VGA text buffer with volatile writes, formatting without an allocator through core::fmt::Write, inline assembly, and how microcontroller crates use memory-mapped registers and the type-state pattern.

RiA 11.1.7 Being power conscious by interacting with the CPU

RiA 11.2.3 Creating a type that can print to the VGA frame buffer
RiA 11.3 Implementing a panic handler that reports the error to the user

blocks.md: Every program so far ran on top of an operating system: `println!` asks the OS to write to a terminal, `Vec` asks an allocator for memory, `thread::spawn` asks the OS for a thread. A kernel, a bootloader or the firmware of a microcontroller has **no OS underneath**. Rust still works there, because the standard library is built in layers and you can stop at the lowest one.

blocks.title: The three layers of the standard library
A freestanding program
blocks.md:
`#![no_std]` at the top of a crate links `core` instead of `std`. A **library** can do this and still be used everywhere; many crates (`serde`, `heapless`) do, so they run on microcontrollers too. A **binary** with no OS also needs:

- **`#![no_main]`**: there is no C runtime to call `main`, so we define the entry point ourselves.
- **an entry point**: the linker looks for a symbol, `_start` on x86, called by the bootloader. It never returns (`-> !`): there is nobody to return to.
- **`#[panic_handler]`**: `std` normally prints the message and unwinds; without it you decide what a panic does, usually print and halt.
- **a target without an OS**, such as `x86_64-unknown-none` or `thumbv7em-none-eabihf` for ARM Cortex-M (`rustup target add ...`).

*Rust in Action* builds **FledgeOS** this way, using the `bootloader` crate and `bootimage` to produce a disk image that boots in the QEMU emulator. Its first version, modernized for the 2024 edition:

blocks.explain: This only builds for a bare-metal target and runs under a bootloader, so it cannot run in the console. The rest of the lesson simulates the hardware in an ordinary program. `hlt` tells the CPU to sleep until an interrupt arrives, instead of spinning at 100%.

blocks.title: VGA text mode
blocks.md: When a PC boots in VGA-compatible text mode, the screen is a grid of **80 × 25** cells, and the hardware reads it from memory starting at address **`0xb8000`**: 2 bytes per cell, 4,000 bytes in all. Writing to that memory changes the screen. This is **memory-mapped I/O** (MMIO): device registers that look like ordinary memory addresses.

blocks.title: One VGA cell
rows: the character, in code page 437 (ASCII plus box drawing)
blink (or bright background, depending on the mode)

blocks.md: *Rust in Action* names the 16 colors with a `#[repr(u8)]` enum, so each variant has a fixed byte value and the compiler rejects colors that do not exist. Writes use **`write_volatile`**. An ordinary write to memory that the program never reads again could be removed by the optimizer; a **volatile** write is always performed, in order, which is what device memory needs. Here the 4,000 bytes are an array so the code can run in the console:

blocks.explain: Each character byte (`0x52` is `R`) is followed by the attribute `0x0b`: bright cyan (`0xB`) on black (`0x0`). In FledgeOS the pointer is `0xb8000 as *mut u8` and the same code paints the screen.

blocks.title: Formatting without std
blocks.md: `println!` is in `std`, but formatting itself is in `core`. Any type that implements **`core::fmt::Write`** (one method, `write_str`) can be the target of `write!`, and `write!` handles `{}` and `{:?}` with no heap allocation. FledgeOS implements it for its cursor, which gives it formatted output and a panic handler that prints the `PanicInfo` message (`write!(cursor, "{}", info)`) before halting. Writing into a fixed buffer shows the idea:

blocks.explain: Nothing here needs an allocator. The `heapless` crate offers `heapless::String<N>` and `Vec<T, N>` built the same way, with capacity fixed at compile time.

blocks.title: Inline assembly
blocks.md: `core::arch::asm!` (stable since Rust 1.59) embeds machine instructions: `asm!("hlt")` to sleep, or instructions with register operands such as `asm!("add {0}, {1}", inout(reg) x, in(reg) y)`. It is always `unsafe`, and it is specific to one CPU architecture, so guard it with `#[cfg(target_arch = "x86_64")]`. *Rust in Action* used the older `core::intrinsics::abort` and LLVM intrinsics, which need nightly Rust.

blocks.title: Bare metal microcontrollers
blocks.md:
*Comprehensive Rust*'s bare-metal days use a micro:bit (an ARM Cortex-M board). The same ideas apply, plus a set of community crates layered like `core` / `alloc` / `std`:

- **`cortex-m-rt`** provides the reset handler and the `#[entry]` attribute for your `fn main() -> !`.
- A **PAC** (peripheral access crate, generated by `svd2rust` from the chip vendor's description) gives a typed, volatile register for every peripheral address.
- A **HAL** crate builds safe drivers (GPIO pins, timers, UART) on top of the PAC, implementing the **`embedded-hal`** traits so device drivers work on any chip.
- **`#[global_allocator]`** plus `extern crate alloc` brings back `Vec` and `Box` when you have spare RAM.

HALs model hardware states as types, the **type-state pattern** from chapter 18: a pin is `Pin<Input>` or `Pin<Output>`, and only an output pin has `set_high`. Configuring the pin consumes the old value, so using it in the wrong mode does not compile.

blocks.output:
pin 21 configured as output
pin 21 high
size of a pin: 1 byte
blocks.explain: `PhantomData<Mode>` takes no space, so the type-state costs nothing at run time: the check happened at compile time.

blocks.title: Newlines and wrapping on a tiny screen
blocks.md: The screen is 12 cells wide and 3 rows high; each cell is a `u16` holding the attribute in the high byte and the character in the low byte. `write_byte` currently writes every byte in a row. Make `\n` move to the start of the next row, and make a byte that would go past the end of a row wrap to the next one.
hints: Add a `newline` method that does `self.row += 1; self.col = 0;`.
Wrap before writing: `if self.col == W { self.newline(); }`. Checking after writing would wrap one byte too early for a line that exactly fills the row.

blocks.title: A no_std VGA text writer
blocks.goal: Write the screen driver of a tiny kernel as a no_std library: colors, cells, wrapping, scrolling and core::fmt::Write.
blocks.behavior:
The crate starts with `#![cfg_attr(not(test), no_std)]`, so only `core` is available outside tests. Implement:
- `pub fn attribute(fg: Color, bg: Color) -> u8`: background in the high 4 bits, foreground in the low 4.
- `pub fn cell(ch: u8, attr: u8) -> u16`: attribute in the high byte, character in the low byte.
- `Writer::new(buf, width, height)`: panics if `buf.len() != width * height`; fills the buffer with blank cells (`b' '` in attribute `0x07`, gray on black), which is also the starting attribute; cursor at row 0, column 0.
- `set_color(fg, bg)`, `position() -> (row, col)`.
- `write_byte(b)`: `\n` goes to the next row; printable ASCII (`0x20..=0x7e`) is written as is and any other byte as `0xfe` (a block). If the cursor is past the end of the row (`col == width`), wrap first. Going to the next row from the last row **scrolls**: every row moves up one, and the last row becomes blank cells in the current attribute.
- `clear()`: blank cells in the current attribute, cursor to (0, 0).
- `impl core::fmt::Write for Writer` writing each byte of the string.
hints: Write a private `newline(&mut self)`: if `row + 1 < height`, move down; otherwise `self.buf.copy_within(width.., 0)` and blank the last row.
`match b { b'\n' => ..., 0x20..=0x7e => ..., _ => ... }` covers the three cases.
`write_str` is `for b in s.bytes() { self.write_byte(b) } Ok(())`.
blocks.solution_explain: The writer only borrows a slice of cells, so the same code drives a test buffer or, in a kernel, a slice made from `0xb8000` (where you would switch the stores to `write_volatile`). Scrolling is one `copy_within` plus a `fill`. Wrapping lazily, only when the next byte arrives, keeps an exactly full line from leaving an empty row behind it.

questions.q: Which crate is available with `#![no_std]` and no allocator?
questions.explanation: core needs nothing from the platform.

questions.q: Why does a freestanding binary need `#![no_main]`?
options: No runtime calls main; we define the entry point such as _start

questions.q: Why use `write_volatile` for the VGA buffer?
options: The optimizer might remove ordinary writes the program never reads back
It is the only safe write
questions.explanation: Device memory has side effects the compiler cannot see.

questions.q: What is the attribute byte for yellow (0xE) on blue (0x1)?
questions.explanation: Background in the high nibble, foreground in the low.

points: std = core + alloc + the OS layer; no_std code uses core, plus alloc if you provide an allocator.
A freestanding binary needs no_main, an entry point such as _start that never returns, and a #[panic_handler].
VGA text mode is 80x25 two-byte cells at 0xb8000: character, then attribute.
Use write_volatile for memory-mapped I/O; #[repr(u8)] enums give names to hardware values.
core::fmt::Write gives formatted output with no heap.
Embedded Rust layers PAC, HAL and embedded-hal traits, and uses type-state to make misuse a compile error.

terms.def: A crate attribute that links core instead of std, for code without an operating system.
A program that runs without an operating system or C runtime.
The function marked #[panic_handler] that decides what a panic does in a no_std program.
Controlling hardware by reading and writing special memory addresses.
A memory read or write the compiler must perform exactly as written.
Hardware abstraction layer: a crate with safe drivers for a chip's peripherals.
